Image Processing · Lab 11 · Material

Geometric Augmentation

MaterialPracticeQuiz

Create varied views of familiar tabletop objects while keeping the learning task meaningful. You will make each random decision inspectable and reproducible.

What you will learn

  • Choose geometric changes that preserve a stated label.
  • Sample bounded geometry with local random generators.
  • Replay recorded parameters without resampling.
  • Keep validation and test preprocessing deterministic.

Before this lab: Use RGB arrays, slicing, resizing and affine transforms from earlier labs.

In this lab

  1. Geometry and Label Meaning
  2. Local Random Generators
  3. Rotation Bounds and Resampling
  4. Translation and Border Evidence
  5. Random Crops and Field of View
  6. Application Probabilities
  7. Parameter Replay
  8. Training and Evaluation Paths

Prepare your notebook

Use a Python notebook with OpenCV, Pillow, NumPy and Matplotlib. Run the setup once, then run the guided blocks in order. The copy button selects only the code.

The examples were checked with OpenCV 4.13, Pillow 12.3, NumPy 2.2 and Matplotlib 3.11. The repository’s Python requirements list the versions. These pages and images open offline; running the code requires the Python libraries.

Run setup once. Fixtures are drawn RGB uint8 arrays in H,W,C order; OpenCV output sizes use (width, height).

Python · shared setup
import json
import tempfile
from pathlib import Path
from io import BytesIO
import numpy as np
import cv2
from PIL import Image, ImageDraw
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
cv2.setNumThreads(1)
rng = np.random.default_rng(211)

# Drawn tabletop fixtures: RGB uint8, H=128, W=160, C=3.
def scene(kind="mug", seed=0):
    local = np.random.default_rng(seed)
    yy, xx = np.mgrid[:128, :160]
    grain = 4 * np.sin(xx / 3) + local.normal(0, 1, (128, 160))
    base = np.stack([205 + yy / 8 + grain, 191 + yy / 10 + grain,
                     166 + yy / 12 + grain], axis=-1)
    canvas = Image.fromarray(np.clip(base, 0, 255).astype(np.uint8))
    draw = ImageDraw.Draw(canvas)
    for y in range(12, 128, 24):
        draw.line((0, y, 159, y), fill=(184, 168, 146), width=1)
    if kind == "mug":
        draw.ellipse((105, 43, 139, 87), fill=(53, 118, 167))
        draw.ellipse((112, 50, 131, 80), fill=(208, 193, 168))
        draw.rounded_rectangle((43, 33, 115, 102), radius=12, fill=(66, 145, 194))
        draw.ellipse((43, 27, 115, 48), fill=(34, 71, 91))
        draw.ellipse((48, 31, 110, 43), fill=(116, 71, 40))
        draw.text((64, 64), "TEA", fill=(245, 246, 237))
    elif kind == "parcel":
        draw.rectangle((27, 31, 123, 101), fill=(174, 117, 65), outline=(70, 45, 28), width=2)
        draw.rectangle((69, 32, 80, 100), fill=(224, 190, 124))
        draw.rectangle((86, 48, 115, 77), fill=(247, 244, 225))
        draw.text((89, 55), "UP", fill=(25, 30, 34))
        draw.line((39, 64, 39, 45), fill=(25, 30, 34), width=3)
        draw.polygon([(33, 48), (45, 48), (39, 41)], fill=(25, 30, 34))
    elif kind == "apple":
        draw.ellipse((43, 38, 115, 108), fill=(190, 48, 40))
        draw.ellipse((58, 44, 75, 63), fill=(241, 123, 93))
        draw.line((80, 42, 86, 26), fill=(75, 63, 32), width=5)
        draw.ellipse((84, 25, 104, 35), fill=(54, 117, 56))
    else:
        raise ValueError("Unknown fixture kind")
    return np.asarray(canvas).copy()

def panels(images, titles, cmap=None):
    fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, len(images), figsize=(4 * len(images), 3.4), squeeze=False)
    for ax, image, title in zip(axes[0], images, titles):
        ax.imshow(image, cmap=cmap)
        ax.set_title(title)
        ax.axis("off")
    fig.tight_layout()
    return fig

The image comparisons below come from the guided code. Use their captions and shared display scales to compare each change.

Guided task 01

Geometry and Label Meaning

A geometric augmentation is a proposed new view of an existing example. Its acceptability depends on the target, not on whether the picture remains attractive. Our drawn parcel has text and an upward arrow. A horizontal flip may be acceptable when the target is simply “parcel”, yet it damages an ordinary text-reading task. A vertical flip also changes the arrow's direction. Write the target in words before choosing a policy.

Array slicing can reverse columns or rows without interpolation. The copy makes a separate, contiguous image rather than a negative-stride view. This distinction helps when passing arrays to other libraries or storing a collection of variants. All three images retain height, width and RGB channels; that shape agreement says nothing about whether their labels are still valid. These exercises demonstrate mechanics on drawings, not the distribution of a real camera dataset.

Try it

  1. Draw a labeled parcel.
  2. Reverse columns and then rows separately.
  3. Inspect text and arrow direction against two possible targets.
Python · run in order
original = scene("parcel")
horizontal = original[:, ::-1].copy()
vertical = original[::-1].copy()
fig = panels([original, horizontal, vertical], ["Original parcel", "Horizontal flip", "Vertical flip"])

Read the result

Look at the arrow and printed UP separately from the box outline. The same operation can preserve object identity while invalidating a direction or reading label; a valid policy needs that distinction before any random sampling.

Change and compare

  • Compare the policy for parcel identity with arrow-direction recognition.
  • Repeat with the mug and identify what happens to its printed word.

Guided task 02

Local Random Generators

A seed initializes a sequence of draws; it does not attach a permanent transformation to an image by itself. Recreating a generator with the same seed and issuing the same calls reproduces the sequence in this environment. Continuing to use one generator advances it. An extra draw earlier in the pipeline can therefore change all later parameters even when the seed string is unchanged.

Keep the generator local to the sampling function or pass it explicitly. Here it chooses an integer horizontal displacement in the inclusive interval from −12 to 12 pixels. NumPy's upper bound is excluded, so the call ends at 13. The sampled value is then used in a forward translation matrix. Separating sampling from application makes it possible to compare two identical replays without hoping that another piece of code has left global random state untouched.

Try it

  1. Create two generators with seed 211.
  2. Draw one horizontal displacement from each.
  3. Apply both matrices to the same mug.
Python · run in order
a = np.random.default_rng(211)
b = np.random.default_rng(211)
dx_a = int(a.integers(-12, 13))
dx_b = int(b.integers(-12, 13))
mug = scene("mug")
matrix_a = np.float32([[1, 0, dx_a], [0, 1, 0]])
matrix_b = np.float32([[1, 0, dx_b], [0, 1, 0]])
view_a = cv2.warpAffine(mug, matrix_a, (160, 128), borderValue=(225, 218, 200))
view_b = cv2.warpAffine(mug, matrix_b, (160, 128), borderValue=(225, 218, 200))
fig = panels([mug, view_a, view_b], ["Input", f"Seed 211: dx={dx_a}", f"Seed 211 replay: dx={dx_b}"])

Read the result

The two generated views should agree pixel for pixel. This verifies this sequence of operations, rather than guaranteeing identical results across every library version or a reordered pipeline. Store parameters as well as the seed for a durable audit trail.

Change and compare

  • Draw a second displacement from a and compare its position in the sequence.
  • Use a different seed while keeping the displacement bounds unchanged.

Guided task 03

Rotation Bounds and Resampling

Rotation introduces interpolation because most output pixel centers do not land exactly on input centers. Use the image center ((W−1)/2, (H−1)/2) for this center-coordinate operation. OpenCV's positive angle is counterclockwise in the displayed image. We compare a modest 8-degree rotation with a 70-degree stress view, keeping the same output canvas and constant border color.

The stress image is deliberately outside our proposed ±10-degree policy for normally upright tabletop captures. It is useful for learning the effect of the operator, but it should not quietly become a routine training sample. Border triangles and clipped objects are part of the new image, not just display decoration. A larger canvas would change the input contract; repeated rotations would resample the image repeatedly. Record both the angle and the fixed-canvas decision when reviewing a policy.

Try it

  1. Rotate around pixel-center coordinates.
  2. Use linear interpolation and a fixed border color.
  3. Compare the proposed range with a deliberate stress case.
Python · run in order
angles = [8.0, 70.0]
rotated = []
for angle in angles:
    transform = cv2.getRotationMatrix2D((79.5, 63.5), angle, 1.0)
    rotated.append(cv2.warpAffine(mug, transform, (160, 128), flags=cv2.INTER_LINEAR, borderValue=(225, 218, 200)))
fig = panels([mug] + rotated, ["Original", "8 degrees: candidate", "70 degrees: stress only"])

Read the result

Inspect the rim, printed word and table edges. Shape preservation, interpolation softness and semantic plausibility are different questions. No score from a future classifier has been measured here, so the comparison supports policy inspection only.

Change and compare

  • Change the modest angle to −8 degrees and compare border placement.
  • Use nearest interpolation once to inspect edge stair steps on RGB content.

Guided task 04

Translation and Border Evidence

Moving an object in a fixed canvas creates positions with no source pixels. Constant padding states this honestly through a chosen fill. Reflection padding can look smoother, but it fabricates mirrored content at the border. Either choice can become a clue that a downstream model exploits. The choice belongs in the preprocessing contract, especially when the real capture system has a characteristic background.

Translate a parcel 18 pixels right and 6 pixels down. Warp a separate all-ones coverage array with the same matrix and nearest interpolation. Its zeros identify locations that came from padding; they are not a segmentation label for the object. Inspecting this coverage separates an intended coordinate shift from an accidental change in how missing pixels were filled. For this integer translation, the retained source rectangle has width 142 and height 122.

Try it

  1. Build the forward translation matrix.
  2. Compare constant and reflected padding.
  3. Warp a coverage array to locate non-source pixels.
Python · run in order
translation = np.float32([[1, 0, 18], [0, 1, 6]])
constant = cv2.warpAffine(original, translation, (160, 128), borderValue=(225, 218, 200))
reflected = cv2.warpAffine(original, translation, (160, 128), borderMode=cv2.BORDER_REFLECT_101)
coverage = cv2.warpAffine(np.ones((128, 160), np.uint8), translation, (160, 128), flags=cv2.INTER_NEAREST, borderValue=0)
fig = panels([constant, reflected, coverage], ["Constant border", "Reflected border", "Source coverage: 1"])

Read the result

The coverage image is a geometric diagnostic shared by both RGB border choices. Reflection can copy parts of a nearby object, so a plausible-looking edge is not evidence that the picture represents a physically observed scene.

Change and compare

  • Move the parcel left instead and locate the new padding strip.
  • Measure the padded fraction for a 9-pixel horizontal shift with no vertical shift.

Guided task 05

Random Crops and Field of View

A crop followed by resizing is not just a translation: it changes the visible field of view and the object's apparent size. First choose crop dimensions, then sample a valid top-left origin. A 112-by-144 crop of our 128-by-160 array permits top offsets 0 through 16 and left offsets 0 through 16. Slicing uses rows before columns, while resize receives width before height.

This policy removes only a narrow border around our centered apple fixture. That makes the example easy to inspect, but another dataset could contain an object against an edge. Cropping a target out while retaining its classification label creates an inconsistent example. A segmentation or detection task also requires transformed annotations, covered in the alignment lesson. Here we explicitly inspect retention instead of assuming that every legal array slice is a legal training sample.

Try it

  1. Sample valid top and left offsets.
  2. Slice a 112-row by 144-column crop.
  3. Resize to the original canvas with linear interpolation.
Python · run in order
crop_rng = np.random.default_rng(312)
top = int(crop_rng.integers(0, 17))
left = int(crop_rng.integers(0, 17))
apple = scene("apple")
crop = apple[top:top+112, left:left+144]
crop_view = cv2.resize(crop, (160, 128), interpolation=cv2.INTER_LINEAR)
fig = panels([apple, crop, crop_view], ["Input", f"Crop at ({left}, {top})", "Resized crop"])

Read the result

The apple occupies a larger proportion of the final canvas. Compare stem and lower edge visibility, not only array shape. Different horizontal and vertical resize factors also alter proportions slightly because this crop does not exactly match the original aspect ratio.

Change and compare

  • Choose an aspect-preserving 104-by-130 crop and compare proportions.
  • Place a crop boundary through the apple to explain why the identity label becomes questionable.

Guided task 06

Application Probabilities

A probability controls whether an operation is applied; it does not specify a fixed quota in each batch. With flip probability 0.35, a small collection need not contain exactly 35 percent flipped images. Sample a uniform value in [0,1) and compare it with the threshold. Keep the Boolean decision so the observed count can be audited alongside the pictures.

The example creates 20 apple views and displays the first four. An apple-identity label can tolerate horizontal reflection in this simplified setting, whereas a left-versus-right handle target could not. Repeated appearances of an unchanged image are legitimate outcomes of this policy. If the design requires exactly seven flips in a collection of twenty, that is a different sampling procedure with dependent decisions. Do not describe a probability policy as a guarantee about each finite group.

Try it

  1. Draw 20 independent threshold decisions with seed 411.
  2. Apply column reversal only when the decision is true.
  3. Inspect sample views and report the observed count.
Python · run in order
policy_rng = np.random.default_rng(411)
decisions = policy_rng.random(20) < 0.35
views = [apple[:, ::-1].copy() if decision else apple.copy() for decision in decisions]
fig = panels(views[:4], [f"View {i}: flip={bool(decisions[i])}" for i in range(4)])
fig.suptitle(f"{int(decisions.sum())} flips among 20 draws; configured p=0.35")
fig.tight_layout()

Read the result

A count different from seven is not a bug by itself. Verify the threshold and seeded decisions first, then inspect a larger sample if you need a more stable estimate of the policy's application frequency.

Change and compare

  • Compare 20 and 2000 draws without changing the threshold.
  • Set probability to zero and then one to verify boundary behavior.

Guided task 07

Parameter Replay

Reproducibility is easier to inspect when the sampled choices are ordinary data. Record a flip decision, angle and horizontal displacement, then apply those values without asking the random generator anything else. JSON can store these scalars, but NumPy scalar types should be converted to Python bool, float or int first. The record also states operation order and interpolation.

The replay function below flips first, then applies one rotation matrix with an added horizontal translation. Adding to the final matrix offset means translation in output coordinates after rotation. Reversing those operations would generally produce another result. Exact equality after a JSON round trip verifies that the same implementation uses the same parameters. This compact record relies on this exact application function, which fixes the canvas, center rule and border color. Retain that code, the library versions and original input for replay; the record alone is not a portable transform specification.

Try it

  1. Sample one plain-data parameter record.
  2. Apply flip followed by rotation and translation.
  3. Serialize and replay the record without additional randomness.
Python · run in order
replay_rng = np.random.default_rng(512)
record = {"flip": bool(replay_rng.random() < 0.4), "angle": float(replay_rng.uniform(-9, 9)), "dx": int(replay_rng.integers(-8, 9)), "order": "flip_then_affine", "interpolation": "linear"}
def apply_record(image, record):
    base = image[:, ::-1].copy() if record["flip"] else image.copy()
    h, w = image.shape[:2]
    transform = cv2.getRotationMatrix2D(((w-1)/2, (h-1)/2), record["angle"], 1.0)
    transform[0, 2] += record["dx"]
    return cv2.warpAffine(base, transform, (w, h), flags=cv2.INTER_LINEAR, borderValue=(225, 218, 200))
first = apply_record(apple, record)
restored_record = json.loads(json.dumps(record))
replayed = apply_record(apple, restored_record)
fig = panels([apple, first, replayed], ["Original", "Recorded view", "JSON replay"])

Read the result

Look for identical edges and padding in the two augmented panels. The function has no random calls, making the replay independent of what the surrounding notebook has sampled since the record was created.

Change and compare

  • Advance replay_rng by 100 draws and replay the same record again.
  • Change only dx in a copied record and inspect which parts of the result move.

Guided task 08

Training and Evaluation Paths

Assign independent object groups before generating related views. A transformed view is still evidence from its original object, so it must retain that group's split. In this small demonstration, groups 0–3 are training, group 4 is validation and group 5 is test. These explicit assignments illustrate the rule without pretending that six drawings form a useful benchmark.

Training may sample a fresh bounded translation when an example is requested. Evaluation follows a fixed resize and scaling path so repeated measurements would refer to the same inputs. It should not consume training randomness. We keep that distinction visible in separate functions, rather than placing a random call outside an if statement that later discards its result. Do not tune the augmentation range through repeated test inspection. This lesson stops at input preparation; no model performance is inferred from these pictures.

Try it

  1. Keep explicit group sets disjoint.
  2. Use bounded random translation only in training.
  3. Call deterministic evaluation twice and compare the arrays.
Python · run in order
split_groups = {"train": {0, 1, 2, 3}, "validation": {4}, "test": {5}}
def training_view(image, local):
    dx = int(local.integers(-6, 7))
    transform = np.float32([[1, 0, dx], [0, 1, 0]])
    shifted = cv2.warpAffine(image, transform, (160, 128), borderValue=(225, 218, 200))
    return cv2.resize(shifted, (120, 96), interpolation=cv2.INTER_AREA).astype(np.float32) / 255.0
def evaluation_view(image):
    return cv2.resize(image, (120, 96), interpolation=cv2.INTER_AREA).astype(np.float32) / 255.0
train_local = np.random.default_rng(611)
train_view = training_view(scene("apple", 0), train_local)
eval_a = evaluation_view(scene("apple", 4))
eval_b = evaluation_view(scene("apple", 4))
fig = panels([train_view, eval_a, eval_b], ["Training group 0", "Validation group 4", "Same validation call"])

Read the result

Repeated validation calls agree exactly while training has a separately controlled random path. Both paths finish with the same 96-by-120 RGB float32 contract, so a future model receives consistent dimensions and scale regardless of split.

Change and compare

  • Inspect the shared output shape and range after several training translations.
  • Record training parameters per group and verify they never create new split memberships.
